section.title: Faith or Works of the Law
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from his own story to argue directly with the Galatians. He appeals to their experience, they received the Spirit by hearing with faith, and to Scripture, Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness. He shows that all who rely on works of the law are under a curse, and that Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse for us, so that the blessing of Abraham and the Spirit come by faith.
section.thesis: The Galatians received the Spirit and share Abraham's blessing by faith, not by works of the law, for the law brings only a curse on those who fail to keep it; but Christ redeemed us by becoming a curse in our place, so that the blessing promised to Abraham and the gift of the Spirit come to all who believe.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the appeal to experience, you received the Spirit by hearing with faith; the appeal to Abraham, who believed and was counted righteous, so those of faith are his sons; and the curse of the law answered by Christ becoming a curse for us, bringing the blessing and the Spirit.

units.label: The appeal to experience
units.note: did you receive the Spirit by works or by faith

verses.text: O foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you? Before your very eyes Jesus Christ was clearly portrayed as crucified.
I would like to learn just one thing from you: Did you receive the {{pneuma|Spirit}} by works of the law, or by hearing with faith?
Are you so foolish? After starting in the Spirit, are you now finishing in the flesh?
Have you suffered so much for nothing, if it really was for nothing?
Does God lavish His Spirit on you and work miracles among you because you practice the law, or because you hear and believe?

units.label: The appeal to Abraham
units.note: Abraham believed God and it was credited to him

verses.text: So also, “Abraham believed God, and it was {{logizomai|credited}} to him as righteousness.”
Understand, then, that those who have faith are sons of Abraham.
The Scripture foresaw that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, and foretold the gospel to Abraham: “All nations will be blessed through you.”
So those who have faith are blessed along with Abraham, the man of faith.

units.label: The curse borne by Christ
units.note: Christ became a curse for us to bring the blessing

verses.text: All who rely on works of the law are under a {{katara|curse}}. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written in the Book of the Law.”
Now it is clear that no one is justified before God by the law, because, “The righteous will live by faith.”
The law, however, is not based on faith; on the contrary, “The man who does these things will live by them.”
Christ {{exagorazo|redeemed}} us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us. For it is written: “Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree.”
He redeemed us in order that the blessing promised to Abraham would come to the Gentiles in Christ Jesus, so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit.

pneuma.gloss: Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the breath and power of God. Paul appeals to the Galatians' own experience of receiving the Spirit as decisive proof: the Spirit came by hearing with faith, not by keeping the law. The presence of the Spirit is the mark of belonging to God and the down payment of the promised inheritance, and it is given to faith, not to works.

logizomai.gloss: To reckon, to count, to credit to an account. When Abraham believed, God credited righteousness to him, a bookkeeping term: righteousness was reckoned to his account as a gift received by faith, not wages earned by works. This is the pattern for every believer, counted righteous before God on the basis of faith in His promise.

katara.gloss: A curse, the sentence of condemnation. The law pronounces a curse on everyone who fails to keep all of it, and since no one keeps it perfectly, all who rely on the law stand under this curse. The word sets up the stunning reversal of verse 13: Christ took the curse we deserved upon Himself.

exagorazo.gloss: To redeem, to buy out, to purchase and set free, as one might buy a slave out of bondage. Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, paying the price with His own death on the tree. Redemption is costly rescue: He took our condemnation so that the blessing and the Spirit could be ours.

basic.context: Paul is exasperated. The Galatians began the Christian life by faith and received the Spirit through the gospel, yet now they are being persuaded that they must keep the law to complete what grace began. Paul argues from their own experience and from Abraham that righteousness and the Spirit come by faith. Then he shows that the law only curses lawbreakers, and that Christ took that curse for us.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul reasons like a lawyer, stacking arguments: your experience, the Scriptures about Abraham, the curse of the law, and the cross. Notice how he reads the Old Testament as pointing to justification by faith all along. Read this as the case for grace built from the Bible itself.
basic.originalLanguages: The Galatians received the pneuma, the Spirit, by faith, not works. Abraham believed and righteousness was logizomai, credited, to him. The law brings a katara, a curse, on all who fail to keep it, and Christ exagorazo, redeemed us, buying us out of that curse by becoming a curse for us.
basic.typology: Abraham is the pattern of the believer, justified by faith long before the law was given. The curse of hanging on a tree, from Deuteronomy, finds its fulfillment in Christ crucified. The promise that all nations would be blessed through Abraham is fulfilled as the blessing and the Spirit reach the Gentiles in Christ.
basic.christ: Christ is portrayed as crucified before their very eyes, and He is the one who redeemed us from the curse by becoming a curse for us. He hung on the tree under the sentence we deserved, so that the blessing promised to Abraham and the gift of the Spirit could flow to all who believe. His cross is the hinge of the whole argument.
basic.god: God credits righteousness to those who believe, as He did with Abraham. God pours out His Spirit and works miracles in response to faith, not law keeping. God had planned from the beginning to justify the Gentiles by faith, announcing the gospel to Abraham. He is a God who blesses through promise and faith.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 15 records Abraham believing God and being counted righteous. Habakkuk 2 says the righteous will live by faith. Deuteronomy 21 speaks of the curse on one hung on a tree, fulfilled at the cross.
basic.oneStory: The promise to Abraham, that all nations would be blessed through him, drives the whole Bible forward. Here it lands: through Christ who bore the curse, the blessing and the Spirit come to the nations by faith. The gospel was preached to Abraham long ago and is now fulfilled in Jesus.

context.literary:
Verses 1 to 14 are built as a courtroom speech with three witnesses called in turn: the Galatians' own experience, verses 1 to 5; Abraham, verses 6 to 9; and the law itself, verses 10 to 14. The opening is a volley of five questions, the Spirit appearing in the first and the last of them, verses 2 and 5, which frames the unit. Paul does not argue about the Spirit; he asks them to remember what happened. The word 'foolish' is repeated in verses 1 and 3, a sharp rebuke from a man who elsewhere calls them brothers.

The central section turns on the pair 'blessing' and 'curse.' Blessing runs through verses 8, 9 and 14, curse through verses 10 and 13, and the two meet at the cross. The middle movement is held together by four Scripture quotations in verses 10 to 13, taken from Deuteronomy 27:26, Habakkuk 2:4, Leviticus 18:5 and Deuteronomy 21:23. Together with the Genesis quotations of verses 6 and 8, Paul calls six witnesses from the law and the prophets, and he lets the Old Testament do most of the talking. The structure is a chain, each link supplying what the next needs: Abraham's faith, the Gentiles' blessing, the law's curse, the cross as the exchange, and the Spirit as the result.

The unit also has a clear beginning and end. It opens with Christ 'portrayed as crucified' and ends with Christ redeeming us so that we 'receive the promise of the Spirit.' Between them the whole of the gospel is laid out in small. Verse 14 states a double purpose, introduced by two clauses beginning 'in order that' and 'so that,' so that the cross is shown to have two aims, the blessing reaching the nations and the Spirit reaching believers. These will be taken up again in 3:15-29 and 4:1-7.
context.historical:
Paul's readers were converts from paganism, as 4:8 will show, living in the Roman province of Galatia. Which communities he means, whether the churches of the south that Paul planted on his first journey or those further north, is debated and does not change the argument. What matters is that they had received the gospel in a setting where crucifixion was a familiar sight. It was the punishment reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals, and the Roman world regarded it as shameful. To proclaim a crucified man as Lord was to say something that sounded absurd, 1 Corinthians 1:23.

The word 'bewitched' draws on a belief in the evil eye, a malign gaze that could harm a person. Paul uses it half in irony: some power has cast a spell on them, though the real offence is the persuasion of the teachers. The language of 'before your very eyes' picks up the image of a public notice posted for all to read, as if the cross had been nailed up in their streets by Paul's preaching.

The Jewish background is the law's treatment of an executed man. Deuteronomy 21:22-23 required that a body hung on a tree be taken down before nightfall, so that the land would not be defiled, and called such a man cursed. In Jesus' day some Jewish writers read this law as applying to crucifixion, which is how Paul can quote it. The link is made in Acts 5:30 and 10:39, where Peter speaks of Jesus as hung on a tree. John 19:31 notes that the Jewish authorities asked for the bodies to be taken down before the Sabbath, an echo of the same concern. The first hearers, Jewish or Gentile, would have grasped that to say Christ became a curse was no small claim.
context.canonical:
The passage is a tapestry of Old Testament texts, each quoted with care. Genesis 15:6 is the verse on which Paul builds, and he treats it as the founding statement of how God accepts a person. Genesis 12:3, quoted in verse 8 along with the echoes of Genesis 18:18 and 22:18, gives the purpose of the promise, that all nations would be blessed. Habakkuk 2:4, in verse 11, was written in a time of crisis, when the prophet was told to wait for God's vision, and the righteous person's life is marked by trust. Hebrews 10:38 and Romans 1:17 quote the same line, which shows it was a standard text in the early church.

Deuteronomy 27:26 closes the list of curses spoken at Mount Ebal and, in the setting of Deuteronomy 28 to 30, sets out what happens when the nation breaks the covenant. Leviticus 18:5, in verse 12, promises life to the one who keeps God's statutes, and Paul reads it as describing the principle of law, doing and living, in contrast to the principle of faith. Romans 10:5-9 handles the same verse alongside the word of faith.

Forward from the passage, the cross as an exchange is picked up in 2 Corinthians 5:21, where God made the sinless Christ to be sin for us, and 1 Peter 2:24, where He bore our sins on the tree. The 'promise of the Spirit' links to Joel 2:28-29, Ezekiel 36:26-27 and Isaiah 44:3, and is fulfilled at Pentecost, Acts 2:33. The sonship that this blessing creates is the subject of Galatians 4:4-7 and Romans 8:14-17. Revelation 7:9 shows the promise to Abraham at last complete, with people from every nation standing before the throne.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants his readers to feel the absurdity of their position and then be restored to the ground on which they began. The sharp questions are meant to wake them, not to wound. By asking how they received the Spirit, he calls on something they cannot deny, since the experience was theirs, and by asking whether they now think to finish by their own effort what began by God's gift, he exposes the logic of their drift as a form of self-reliance.

He then wants them to see that the Scriptures they are being taught from by the new teachers actually support him. The Abraham of Genesis 15 is exactly the figure the rival teachers must have used, since Abraham was the first to be circumcised, Genesis 17. Paul goes back behind that to Genesis 15:6, when Abraham was counted righteous before circumcision existed. The point is not that Abraham's obedience was irrelevant, but that his standing before God was settled by trust.

The most startling intention is in verses 10 to 14. Paul wants them to see that going back to the law as a way of life is not neutral. It puts them under a sentence, which only the cross can lift. He wants the cross to look as costly as it was, and as complete. He does not expect that they will understand every step of the argument at once, but that they will see it ends where it began, with Christ crucified, and with the Spirit as the proof that God has already accepted them.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The passage describes what happened to the Galatians when they first believed, namely that the Spirit came with power and miracles among them, and it is not a promise that every believer will see miracles. What is prescriptive is the pattern of source: the Spirit is received by hearing with faith and not by effort. That applies to every believer in every place.

Paul's method of reading Scripture is descriptive of how an apostle, taught by the risen Christ, reads the Old Testament, and it is not a licence to find Christ in every verse. He quotes particular texts for particular reasons, and the careful reader will check each one, as the BSB footnotes help us to do. What is prescriptive is the principle that the Old Testament does speak of Christ and the nations, and that its commands, particularly the curses, find their place in the story that ends at the cross.

The statement that Christ became a curse for us describes an event of unique significance and gives no pattern to imitate. Believers are called to take up their crosses, but they do not bear the curse. What follows from it for us is a settled confidence: since the curse has been borne, no one who is in Christ needs to fear it. And since the Spirit is the sign of acceptance, we are to look to Christ as the source of life and not to our own record.

debates.question: What does 'hearing with faith' in verses 2 and 5 mean?

views.label: Hearing that is believing
views.case: The Greek phrase akoe pisteos is a short expression of two nouns, and the BSB takes it as the act of hearing that responds in faith. The contrast is between what the Galatians did, hearing and trusting, and what the law asks, works. Paul's question is who did the work in conversion.

views.label: The message that is believed
views.case: Others take akoe as 'the message' and read the phrase as 'the message of faith,' the content of the gospel preached to them. This fits the way Romans 10:16-17 uses akoe for the report that is heard, and the way Paul says faith comes from hearing.

debates.bearing: Both readings keep the same contrast. Whether the stress is on the act of believing or on the message believed, the Spirit came as a gift received, not a wage earned.

debates.question: Why does the law bring a curse in verse 10, and what does Christ's becoming a curse mean?

views.label: No one keeps all the law, so all stand condemned
views.case: The text quotes 'Cursed is everyone who does not continue to do everything written,' and adds in verse 11 that no one is justified by the law. The unstated step is that no one does everything, which Paul argues in Romans 3:9-20. On this reading Christ bore the penalty that each person deserved, as 2 Corinthians 5:21 and 1 Peter 2:24 say.

views.label: Israel as a nation lay under the exile curse
views.case: Others stress the setting of Deuteronomy 27 to 30, where the curse is the covenant sanction that sent Israel into exile. On this view Christ, as Israel's representative, took the covenant curse on Himself so that the blessing promised to Abraham could go out to the nations. Many holding this view also affirm that He bore the penalty for sin.

debates.bearing: The two readings share the main affirmation: the curse fell on the One who did not deserve it, in the place of those who did, and its removal opens the way for the Gentiles to receive the blessing. The difference is how much weight to put on the national story and how much on individual guilt.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb 'bewitched' in verse 1 is baskaino, the word for casting the evil eye on someone, to harm by an envious or malicious look. It appears only here in the New Testament, but the idea was well known in the ancient world, and Paul uses it with a touch of irony, as if to say that nothing less than a spell could explain such foolishness. What follows is the surprising reply to the spell: Christ publicly displayed before their eyes. The verb for 'portrayed,' prographo, is built from 'write' with the prefix 'before,' and can mean either to write ahead of time or to post publicly, as a notice is displayed. Paul is saying that the crucifixion was set out in front of them as plainly as a poster in a public square.

In verse 3, 'finishing' is the verb epiteleo, which means to bring a work to completion. Its sense is of a builder who brings the roof onto a house. The contrast is between beginning with the Spirit and ending with the flesh, and the form is naturally read as 'are you now being completed,' so that the Galatians are allowing themselves to be finished by some other agent. The suggestion of the verb is that the Christian life is never a Spirit-started, self-finished project.

In verse 5 the participle 'lavish' is epichoregeo, from the older choregos, the wealthy citizen who paid for a chorus at a public festival. The verb carries the idea of generous and abundant provision, and its present tense suggests a supply that is continuing. The 'works miracles' that follow translates the plural dynameis, acts of power, again a present participle. God is still giving, and His giving is on the same terms as it began.

The little phrase ek pisteos, 'by faith' or 'of faith,' occurs repeatedly in verses 7, 8, 9 and 11, and Paul uses ek nomou, 'of law,' in contrast. These are descriptions of a way of life and a source. The people 'of faith' are those whose identity and standing come from faith. It is the verb kremamai, 'hung,' in verse 13 that Paul takes from Deuteronomy 21:23. The Greek Old Testament there reads that the hanged man is cursed by God, but Paul does not repeat the words 'by God.' He lets the point stand that the One hung on the tree bore the curse, without suggesting that Jesus was cursed in His own person.

typology.type: Abraham's faith counted as righteousness, Genesis 15:6
typology.fulfillment: Abraham stood under the stars and believed the promise of descendants, and God counted it to him as righteousness. Paul reads this as the pattern for all who are justified. The correspondence is that of trust in a word from God, and the escalation is that the promise now has its content in Christ. Romans 4:23-25 says the words were written for us who believe in Him who raised Jesus from the dead. The type falls short because Abraham believed a promise yet to be fulfilled, while we believe a promise already kept in the cross and the empty tomb.

typology.type: The hung man and the setting sun, Deuteronomy 21:22-23
typology.fulfillment: The law required that an executed body hung on a tree be taken down before nightfall, because the man was under God's curse and must not defile the land. Joshua 10:26-27 shows the practice with the five kings. Jesus died under that sign: John 19:31 records that the bodies were taken down before the Sabbath, and Acts 13:29 says they took Him down from the tree. In Christ the curse is not just observed but borne for others, as Galatians 3:13 says. The type falls short because the hanged men of Deuteronomy bore their own guilt, while Christ bore ours.

typology.type: The blessing to all nations, Genesis 12:3
typology.fulfillment: God told Abraham that in him all the families of the earth would be blessed, and Paul calls this the gospel announced in advance. The correspondence is the gathering of nations, and Acts 3:25-26 shows Peter applying the promise to the sending of Jesus. In Christ it moves from promise to fact, as Gentiles receive the Spirit by faith. Revelation 7:9 shows it complete in the multitude from every nation. The type falls short in that Abraham's family was at first one nation; the family now is not bounded by ethnicity.

typology.type: The promise of the Spirit, Ezekiel 36:26-27
typology.fulfillment: God promised through the prophets to put His Spirit within His people and to give a new heart. Joel 2:28-29 spoke of the Spirit poured out on all flesh. Paul says that the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles 'so that by faith we might receive the promise of the Spirit,' and Acts 2:16-18 shows Peter claiming Pentecost as the fulfilment of Joel. The escalation is that the Spirit is no longer given to selected leaders for a task but to every believer as a permanent presence. The type is still in progress, since Romans 8:23 says we await the full redemption of our bodies.

study.christ:
Everything in the passage is hung on a single image, Christ crucified, and Paul claims that the preaching of the cross was so vivid that it was as if he had posted it in public. The crucified Christ is the answer to every question in the chapter. He is the reason the Spirit has come, as 3:14 shows. He is the one in whom Abraham's blessing reaches the nations, and He is the one who stands in the place of the cursed.

The central exchange of verse 13 deserves careful reading. Paul says that Christ redeemed us 'by becoming a curse for us,' which goes beyond saying that He suffered a cursed death. The words are 'for us,' hyper hemon, on our behalf, and the whole of the thought is that He took on Himself the sentence that fell on us. 2 Corinthians 5:21 puts it with the same shock, that God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us. Paul guards the truth by taking a text of Deuteronomy, which names the man as cursed by God, and applying it to the cross without suggesting that Jesus deserved it. It is a statement about substitution and not about His character.

The promise of the Spirit is the other side of the exchange. Christ takes the curse so that we may receive the blessing, and the Spirit is the blessing in its most personal form. The Galatians' own experience is therefore an argument for the cross. If they received the Spirit, they received the fruit of Christ's death, and to turn aside to the law would be to abandon the very ground on which God had accepted them.

Verse 16 of this chapter will go on to say that the promise was made to Abraham's seed, 'who is Christ.' So even here the figure of Abraham points ahead. The man who believed God stands in a line that ends in the One in whom all nations are blessed. It should be said that the link between Christ and the passage is not a matter of forced allegory. It is the plain course of Paul's own argument, from Abraham's faith, through the cross, to the Spirit. Where later readers have been tempted to find hidden pictures of Christ in every detail of the Old Testament, Paul himself has chosen a few clear places, and the reader should follow him there.
study.god:
The God of this passage gives freely and does not sell. He pours out His Spirit and works miracles among the Galatians, and Paul asks on what basis. The answer in verse 5 is plain: on the ground of hearing with faith. That is a window into God's character. He is a giver whose gifts are not paid for, and the generosity of the verb 'lavish' tells us the supply is abundant. For worship this means that the proper response to His gifts is gratitude and trust, not the effort to deserve them.

He is also a God who keeps a promise made long ago. Verse 8 says that the Scripture 'foresaw' that God would justify the Gentiles by faith and 'foretold the gospel to Abraham.' The plan did not change when the law arrived, and the gospel did not begin at Pentecost. The same God who spoke to Abraham in Genesis 12 acts in Christ, and His faithfulness runs across the centuries. That is a basis for trusting Him with our own long waits.

The passage holds two things together that can seem at odds: the justice of God and His mercy. The law's curse is real. Paul does not say it was an empty threat, and the quotation from Deuteronomy 27:26 stands as the word of a holy God. Yet the same God provides the redeemer. The curse is not set aside by lowering the standard but by bearing it, and the one who bears it is God's own Son. This is how God can be 'just and the one who justifies,' as Romans 3:26 says.

Finally, God is shown as the one who gathers the nations. The blessing of Abraham was always meant for the Gentiles, and verse 14 says that is why Christ redeemed us. The One who made the nations has never forgotten them, and His purposes in the cross are wide. The Spirit's gift to Gentile believers is the proof that He has accepted them. For readers today, this means that no group is outside His intention, and that no church should treat any group as less than full participants in His promise.

crossReferences.note: The verse Paul builds on in verse 6. It comes after God's promise of descendants and stands before the covenant of circumcision in Genesis 17, so Abraham was counted righteous while still uncircumcised.
The original promise that all the families of the earth would be blessed through Abraham. Paul quotes it in verse 8 and treats it as the gospel announced in advance, long before the law or the cross.
The last of the curses spoken at Mount Ebal, which Paul quotes in verse 10. The setting is covenant renewal, and the curse falls on whoever fails to confirm the words of the law by doing them.
The prophet is told that the righteous will live by his faith while the proud are not upright. Paul takes it in verse 11 as proof that life comes by trusting, not by law-keeping.
The promise of life to the one who keeps God's statutes, quoted in verse 12. Paul uses it to show that law works on a principle of doing, which is a different principle from faith.
The law of the hung man, quoted in verse 13. A body hung on a tree was not to remain overnight, and the man was called cursed. Paul takes this as describing the death Jesus died.

A fuller account of Genesis 15:6 along the same lines. Abraham did not earn his standing, and God justifies the ungodly. It explains what 'credited' means in Galatians 3:6, a gift received and not a wage paid.
Leviticus 18:5 again, set beside the word of faith, which is near us, in our mouth and our heart. The same contrast between doing and believing that Paul draws in Galatians 3:12.
The same exchange stated in other words: God made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us so that we might become the righteousness of God in Him. It confirms that the substitution is meant.
Peter says that Christ bore our sins in His body on the tree. The language of the tree, the same as Deuteronomy 21:23, shows that the early church read the cross in these terms.

Peter says that the exalted Jesus received from the Father the promised Holy Spirit and poured it out. This is the fulfilment of the promise of the Spirit that Galatians 3:14 sets as the goal of the cross.
The writer quotes Habakkuk 2:4 to urge endurance, adding that God has no pleasure in the one who shrinks back. It shows how the same verse works in Paul's argument and in another New Testament voice.

study.oneStory:
Genesis 12 stands behind this passage as the hinge of the whole Bible. After Babel the nations were scattered, and after the fall humanity was cursed. God's answer is to call one man and to promise that through him the families of the earth would be blessed. From that point the story is a story of promise, and everything else is measured against it. Paul's claim in this passage is that the promise has been kept, and that the way to its blessing has been by faith from the beginning.

The curse and the blessing of verses 10 to 14 take us back to the beginning. In Genesis 3 the ground was cursed because of Adam, and the whole creation was subjected to futility, Romans 8:20. At Sinai and again on the plains of Moab, Israel heard the blessings and curses of the covenant, Deuteronomy 28. The prophets saw the curses fall in the exile. What Paul says is that at the cross the curse was gathered up and carried by one man, and that the blessing could now flow to the world. Isaiah 53:5-6 had prophesied such a servant who would be wounded for our transgressions.

What the passage sets up is the full account of the family of Abraham in the rest of the chapter and the sonship of chapter 4. The Spirit is the sign that the new age has come. Joel and Ezekiel had promised that God would one day put His Spirit within His people, and the Galatians had received it. They were living in the age of the promise without knowing how much they had been given.

The story ends where the promise points. In Revelation 7:9-10 a multitude that no one could count from every nation, tribe, people and language stands before the throne. Revelation 22:3 says that there will no longer be any curse. The line from Genesis 3 to Revelation 22 runs through the tree on which Christ was hung, and Paul says it is the same tree that makes the blessing possible for all who believe.

sermon.title: Some Crucial Questions (Galatians 3:1 to 14)
sermon.why: Begg follows Paul's pointed questions to the Galatians, showing that the Spirit and Abraham's blessing come by faith and not by works of the law, and that Christ bore the law's curse in our place to secure the promise.

quiz.q: How did the Galatians first receive the Spirit?

options.text: By hearing with faith, not by works of the law.
options.note: Verse 2 makes their own experience the decisive proof.

options.text: By carefully keeping the law of Moses.
options.note: Paul's point is the opposite; the Spirit came by faith.

options.text: By being circumcised first.
options.note: They received the Spirit before any law keeping, by faith.

options.text: By their own moral effort over time.
options.note: The Spirit was given to faith, not earned by effort.

options.text: Righteousness is credited by faith, so those who believe are his sons.
options.note: Verses 6 and 7 make Abraham the pattern of faith.

options.text: That circumcision is required for righteousness.
options.note: Abraham was counted righteous by faith before circumcision.

options.text: That only physical descendants of Abraham are blessed.
options.note: Those of faith, including Gentiles, are his true children.

options.text: That righteousness is earned by good works.
options.note: It was credited to faith, not earned.

quiz.q: Why are all who rely on works of the law under a curse?

options.text: Because the law curses everyone who fails to keep all of it.
options.note: Verse 10 cites the law's demand for complete obedience.

options.text: Because the law itself is evil.
options.note: The law is not evil; the problem is that no one keeps it fully.

options.text: Because God never gave the law at all.
options.note: God gave the law, but not as the way of justification.

options.text: Because the curse applies only to Gentiles.
options.note: It falls on all who rely on law keeping, Jew or Gentile.

quiz.q: How did Christ deal with the curse of the law?

options.text: He redeemed us by becoming a curse for us, hung on the tree.
options.note: Verse 13 states the substitution at the heart of the gospel.

options.text: He simply cancelled the law so the curse no longer exists.
options.note: He bore the curse Himself rather than merely cancelling it.

options.text: He taught us how to keep the law well enough to avoid it.
options.note: The rescue is His curse bearing death, not better law keeping.

options.text: He left us to bear the curse ourselves.
options.note: He took the curse in our place so we go free.

quiz.q: What was the goal of Christ's redemption in verse 14?

options.text: That Abraham's blessing and the promised Spirit would come by faith.
options.note: The blessing reaches the Gentiles and the Spirit is received by faith.

options.text: That we would finally be able to keep the whole law.
options.note: The goal is the blessing and the Spirit by faith, not law keeping.

options.text: That only Jewish believers would be blessed.
options.note: The blessing explicitly comes to the Gentiles in Christ.

options.text: That the Spirit would be earned by good works.
options.note: The Spirit is received by faith, not earned.

questions: Paul asks whether they began in the Spirit only to finish in the flesh. Where are you tempted to start with grace but then rely on your own effort to grow?
Abraham was counted righteous simply by believing God. How does it steady you to know righteousness is credited, not earned?
Christ became a curse for us. Sit with that exchange for a moment: what does it mean to you that He took the condemnation you deserved?
The Spirit is given to faith, not to law keeping. How have you seen God work in your life in response to simple trust rather than performance?
The blessing of Abraham now reaches all nations in Christ. How does being part of that worldwide family shape the way you see believers unlike you?

translationNotes.note: Credited translates logizomai, an accounting term; righteousness was reckoned to Abraham's account as a gift received by faith, quoting Genesis 15:6.
The righteous will live by faith quotes Habakkuk 2:4; the same text anchors the argument of Romans 1:17.
Cursed is everyone who is hung on a tree quotes Deuteronomy 21:23; Paul applies the curse of the cross to Christ bearing our condemnation.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 3:1-14. Sermon verified this session from the Truth For Life series A Study in Galatians, Volume 1 by Alistair Begg.
